title: Exploring Magnets
intro: Magnets are amazing pieces of metal or stone that can pull other metals towards themselves without touching them. This chapter explores what magnets do, how they behave, and how we use them every day.

branches.label: Earth as a Magnet
details: Earth has its own magnetic field

sections.heading: What Are Magnets?
bullets: A magnet is a piece of material that can attract certain other metals towards itself.
Natural magnets are pieces of magnetite, an ore of iron found in nature.
Most magnets we use are man-made — bar magnets, horseshoe magnets, ring magnets, button magnets.
Magnets can be permanent (stay magnetic for a long time) or temporary (lose magnetism quickly).

sections.heading: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic Materials
bullets: Materials that a magnet can attract are called magnetic materials — iron, nickel, cobalt are common examples.
Materials that a magnet cannot attract are called non-magnetic — wood, plastic, paper, rubber, glass, copper, aluminium.
Steel, which is mostly iron, is also magnetic.
You can sort a mixed pile by simply running a magnet over it — iron pieces stick, others don't.

sections.heading: Poles of a Magnet
bullets: Every magnet has two ends called poles, where its pull is strongest.
The end that points north (when freely hanging) is the north pole (N); the other is the south pole (S).
If you dip a bar magnet into iron filings, the filings cling most thickly at the two ends — showing the poles.
If you cut a magnet in half, each half becomes a complete magnet with its own N and S poles.
You cannot have a magnet with only one pole.

sections.heading: Attraction and Repulsion
bullets: When you bring two magnets close, they either pull towards each other or push apart.
Like poles repel each other — N to N, or S to S.
Unlike poles attract each other — N to S, or S to N.
Repulsion is the surest test of magnetism: only two real magnets can repel each other; an iron piece and a magnet always attract.
The closer two magnets are, the stronger the push or pull.

sections.heading: Making and Caring for Magnets
bullets: You can make a temporary magnet by stroking an iron needle in one direction with one pole of a magnet.
Heating, hammering, or dropping a magnet weakens it.
Magnets should be stored in pairs with unlike poles together and a 'keeper' (a soft iron bar) across the ends.
Keep magnets away from electronic devices like phones and computers — strong fields can affect them.

sections.heading: Earth's Magnetism and the Compass
bullets: Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, with magnetic poles near the geographic poles.
A freely-suspended bar magnet always rests pointing roughly north–south because of Earth's magnetism.
A compass is a small magnet, usually a needle, that pivots freely and shows the north–south direction.
Sailors and travellers have used compasses for hundreds of years to find their way.

sections.heading: Magnets in Daily Life
bullets: Door catches, fridge gaskets, and bag closures use small magnets.
Loudspeakers, headphones, and electric motors all contain magnets.
Hospitals use very strong magnets in MRI machines to take pictures inside the body.
Magnetic strips on bank cards and magnets in computer hard disks store information.
Cranes use big electromagnets in scrapyards to lift heavy iron pieces.

key_takeaways: Magnets attract iron, nickel, and cobalt, but not wood, plastic, or paper.
A magnet has two poles — north and south — where its pull is strongest.
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract; repulsion is the only sure test of magnetism.
Cutting a magnet always gives two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S poles.
Earth itself is a giant magnet, which is why a compass needle points north–south.
Magnets are everywhere — in compasses, motors, speakers, cranes, and medical machines.

glossary.definition: A material that can attract iron and a few other metals without touching them.
A material that is attracted by a magnet, such as iron, nickel, or cobalt.
A material that is not attracted by a magnet, such as wood or plastic.
An end of a magnet where the magnetic pull is strongest.
The end of a freely-suspended magnet that points to Earth's geographic north.
The other end of a magnet, opposite the north pole.
The pulling force between unlike poles or between a magnet and a magnetic material.
The pushing force between two like poles.
A small magnetic needle pivoted to spin freely, used to find the north–south direction.
A naturally occurring iron ore that behaves like a magnet.
